science.title: A hybrid structure based on polycaprolactone nanofibers and propolis-loaded gelatin/hyaluronic acid hydrogel as a cartilage scaffold
science.description: Articular cartilage has a low self-healing capacity due to the lack of blood vessels and nerves. Hybrid structures based on nanofibrous layer incorporating hydrogels can effectively mimic the structure of articular cartilage and stimulate tissue repair. In this study, the electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nanofibers was used to improve the mechanical properties of the hybrid structure. Gelatin was blended with hyaluronic acid at different ratios and loaded with propolis extract as an antibacterial agent to form a hydrogel that served as a substrate for the PCL nanofibrous layer. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) showed that the PCL nanofibers had a uniform, bead-free morphology with an average diameter of 141 ± 25 nm. The images also revealed a strong attachment between the nanofibrous layer and the hydrogel. Contact angle measurements indicated that the presence of hydrophobic PCL nanofibers did not significantly reduce the hydrophilicity of the hybrid. Swelling profiles indicated a swelling ratio of 510 ± 28% for propolis-loaded hybrid. Mechanical testing demonstrated that the incorporation of the PCL web significantly reinforced the hydrogel, with compressive modulus of 67.1 ± 2.36 kPa for the hybrids. The release study showed that approximately 90% of the propolis content was released from the hybrid scaffold containing 10% propolis within 48 h. Antibacterial testing demonstrated high activity of the propolis-loaded scaffolds against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. The MTT assay showed excellent cell viability when cells were exposed to both propolis-loaded and unloaded hybrid scaffolds, especially at concentrations of 5 and 10 µg/mL. In conclusion, the hybrid PCL nanofiber/propolis-loaded gelatin–hyaluronic acid hydrogel represents a promising material for cartilage repair.

science.title: Injection strategy optimization for engineered water enhanced oil recovery in carbonate reservoirs
science.description: Carbonate reservoirs commonly exhibit limited oil recovery because of strong heterogeneity, complex pore structures, and unfavorable wettability. This study presents an integrated experimental-numerical framework for evaluating engineered-water flooding and optimizing injection strategies in the heterogeneous WQ1-57 carbonate reservoir. Laboratory core-flooding experiments were combined with geochemical modeling, multiphase-flow calibration, scale-up, reservoir simulation, and sensitivity analysis. Engineered-water injection consistently enhanced oil displacement, yielding incremental recoveries of 11.7–22.8% across the investigated cores. The calibrated numerical model reproduced the experimental recovery and pressure responses and was subsequently used to evaluate radial, line-drive, and conformance-controlled injection configurations. Among these strategies, conformance-controlled injection provided the most favorable reservoir response, increasing oil recovery by 18.1%, delaying water breakthrough by 0.30 pore volumes, improving areal and vertical sweep by 17% and 20%, respectively, and reducing water cut by 15%. Sensitivity analysis identified horizontal permeability as the dominant control on incremental recovery, followed by residual oil saturation and relative-permeability behavior, whereas engineered-water ionic composition, vertical permeability anisotropy, and injection conditions showed comparatively smaller effects. These findings demonstrate that engineered-water performance is governed by the coupled effects of fluid-rock interactions, reservoir heterogeneity, and injection management.
